utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam -- Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Case IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Indeed, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, you may sit down. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio. I appear for the Prosecution together with my colleague, case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Mr. Wubben will join us later in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my learned friend. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us today our legal assistant Ms. Jasmina Cosic, Miss Adisa Mehic, also our legal assistant, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Before we bring in the witness, any updating on the issues that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just address you in private session about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Tucker. You may sit down. And good morning to you, Colonel Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding and hopefully finish with the cross-examination this morning. I am correct, I hope?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Probably by the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So good morning from me too, and welcome to this larger courtroom. I have a special request from the booths that we go very slowly today. Apparently we were much too fast yesterday, so we need to both make an effort. Now, did you have the opportunity to read the chapter on Srebrenica in Larry Hollingsworth's book?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So thank you for doing that. It's a long chapter, so I don't propose to go into it in any detail, just a few passages which I will deal with now while it's fresh in your memory. Now, Larry Hollingsworth describes there your entry into Srebrenica on the 11th of March, 1993 and how the Belgian truck with the Kevlar lining hit a mine, et cetera. You were present at that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was up with General Morillon, but I personally did not go to the truck after it had blown up, but I heard the explosion and spoke with and interviewed the people who had been there in order to establish what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's at page 187 -- you don't need to have it in front of you, I will just read it -- "My --" this is referring to Hollingsworth. "My heart rate had increased. I was huddled against the window, squinting and peering. This was Srebrenica. The name was known in Washington, New York, in London. Known because no one could get in." Now, obviously that is not literally true because your group got in. But do you agree, first, that when you were in Sarajevo hearing about Srebrenica, that it was famous for being utterly inaccessible?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe it infamous.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, that's probably a better term. And when you were there, did you feel that sense of utter isolation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned radio contacts from Srebrenica with the outside world. Would you agree with this characterisation, that this was no more than, in a way, cries for help to be heard, these broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were definitely cries for help, but there were also other things going on in parallel. They weren't only cries for help. There were other activities going on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, for Bosniaks -- let's bring up Bosniaks now. Obviously UNPROFOR had more freedom of movement, but Srebrenica was completely physically cut off from Tuzla by Serb occupied territory.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on the same page, page 187, I will quote, "Our guide, a small, very friendly man, was in uniform and was introduced as the military commander of the town. That he may have been, but we knew that the real defender of the region was Naser Oric whom we had met in Konjevici." Were you with Larry Hollingsworth at this stage when this military commander was introduced?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was this and when was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This was at the very moment of arrival on the first evening.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we arrived outside the -- what we later came to know was the PTT building, but remember we had just arrived, it was just a building, there were some soldiers who rushed around getting hold of who I later heard were the War Presidency. Yes, there was a man who was described as a local military commander. He was not the overall commander in Srebrenica. I mean, I guess he was the person who was effectively on duty that evening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall someone being introduced to you as the military commander of the town?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was a different person from the mayor?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mayor, and by that I mean Hajrudin Avdic, was never in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now at page 211, and in fact actually it would be -- I think it probably would be helpful if you had it in front of you at this stage. It's Exhibit D218. And just while that is being prepared, I'm going to ask you questions about when the aid convoy came in and then the aid was unloaded and then people were loaded onto the lorries. And if I understand correctly, you were actually at the Serb lines at this point, you weren't actually in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the next morning. General Morillon and I went down to the front line ahead of the departure from Srebrenica of the convoy, so the scenes that Larry describes in there and which I also saw on television reports, I was not present at that. I was actually at the -- the yellow bridge to make sure that the Serbs didn't do anything stupid when the convoy arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. It is page 211 and I understand from your answer that you have read this again last night. But I will read the scene into the record. "I jumped off." That's the lorry. "There was no one from authority in sight. I ran into the PTT building and bounded up the stairs. The mayor was hiding in the room with the stove. I dragged him out and down the stairs. 'What the hell are you going to do about this?' I yelled? In his customary lethargic way he went back into the building and returned with a policeman who began firing into the air with a Kalashnikov rifle. For maybe 30 seconds there was silence and peace, then the mayhem broke out again as family fought family for a place on the trucks. The police tried another burst of fire. It was totally ignored. I pleaded with the mayor to let us at least get the wounded off first, then we would fill up the vehicles, but it was a waste of time. He was powerless. We were all powerless. Mob rule had taken over." And now I appreciate that you weren't personally there when this occurred, but you said you saw it on television and perhaps spoke to the people who witnessed it at firsthand.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And one question again for you as a perhaps the military man: Shooting a rifle into the air is actually quite dangerous, isn't it? In fact, the bullets, as they come down, can injure or kill a person.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But celebratory fire, totally different context. Everybody in the Balkans fired off large amounts of ammunition into the skies with complete disregard for where anything would land.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've spoken of knife fights at air drops of the food, and now we have this scene. Would you agree that in Srebrenica, based on your observations, that it was impossible at that time to control crowds of civilians from fighting for food or fighting for their survival?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking personally, I agree it would be very difficult. However I must also say that if clear leadership had been shown, it would have been more possible. It perhaps would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're aware that when these convoys set off, women were throwing their children onto the lorries and --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It troubled a lot of people. A lot of people who were there said that it affected them very badly, seeing the state that people were in. And I saw these same people in the convoy when they arrived at the yellow bridge and when they met the Serbs effectively for the first time, and they were very, very, very afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see that people actually got crushed to death and asphyxiated on those lorries because of the crush of people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard reports of it, but did not see that in the trucks. I actually accompanied the Serb policemen who climbed up into the back of each truck, because I did not want a Serb to be left alone with the refugees. And when I climbed into the back of each truck, yes, they were very crowded, but the reports which I heard later, I cannot substantiate or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to fix this date, and this would be on what day, the 12th of March?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This would be the day after the convoy came in, so I think it would be the 21st. It would have to be the 21st of March. THE convoy came in on the evening of the 20th and went out on the morning of the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, I missed the reference to the next day. I thought you meant the next day after your arrival. So that is clear. Now if you could turn to page 212, it's the next page, fourth paragraph. There's a quote: "I was just leaving the building when Tony Birtley approached me: "Larry, will you do me a favour. Will you take my films out and give them to ABC in Tuzla. I took them from him and stuffed them in my vest pockets." Now, you told us, I think it was on Monday, about how Tony Birtley's pictures left Srebrenica. So isn't it right that in fact the way they left Srebrenica was by Larry Hollingsworth taking them off someone as a favour of one man to another, indeed one countryman to another. It wasn't as if there was some pouch system involving UNMOs as it seemed to be suggested.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never any pouch system or anything like that. Tony Birtley had in fact asked General Morillon how should he get his tapes out of Srebrenica, and General Morillon said give it to one of the UNMOs or you can give it to someone from UNHCR and I think actually suggested that Larry Hollingsworth would be one of the most reliable people. I would add that, to my belief, that was not the only -- Tony Birtley was passing out a series of tapes and other materials. So was Philipp von Recklinghausen and this was merely one occasion on which they went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it true that it was in fact -- there was a big risk that the Serbs would find these photographs and confiscate them, and that in fact that happened with Philipp von Recklinghausen's photographs, if you know.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment about Philip von Recklinghausen's photographs, but yes, there certainly was risk and we discussed it with Larry and asked him would he be willing to do that, because we believed it was important that the world saw these images.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As I say this is a long chapter so I'm not going to go through it page by page, but having read it, and particularly the description of conditions of life in Srebrenica, is there anything which you would quibble with in terms of that description, or is it consistent with what you saw and heard yourself in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would describe it as remarkably accurate description of the situation there, and many of the things which I have in my diary are almost word-by-word reflected in here, and it is certainly as I remember it and as I have recorded it in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And this has an exhibit number already, so you can just put it to one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's D 218.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, while we're still filling in the picture of life in Srebrenica, I would like to ask you about several topics. The first concerns Srebrenica's fighters, if I can put it that way. Now, concerning the fighting forces in and around Srebrenica, in a statement which you gave to the Prosecution for the Galic case which is dated the first of May 2002, you said in relation to the eastern enclaves, the following. And I needn't put it in front of you, I will just read it and if you disagree, then you can tell me. "While there was certainly some soldiers and civilians in the enclaves who had taken up arms to defend themselves, the vast majority were unarmed civilians." Just for the record, that's page 17, ERN 02192824. Now, do you confirm that is a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, from your observations and experience in Srebrenica, would you agree that the fighters, firstly, didn't stay at barracks but stayed at home with their families and other DPs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or wherever there was any shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that there were no armouries organised and that people just had with them what weapons they possessed or were able to capture from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I saw. I did not see any armouries or any locations where ammunition or weapons were stored, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to put to you what another witness -- I won't say their name -- but said about the organisation or lack of organisation of Srebrenica's armed forces and tell me if you agree on the basis of your intelligence and observations or if you disagree. "It was left up to the people in Srebrenica to decide whether they wanted to be soldiers or not. Because there was no way you could force them to become one. If you wanted to force them to become a soldier, you have to provide them with a gun, with a rifle, and you don't have one. Then the person is going to say, 'Okay, but then you have to provide me with meals, you have to take care of my family, and then I will go and man the positions.' So in essence this was on a voluntary basis, take it or leave it." Now is that consistent with what you saw and observed in Srebrenica of the fighting forces?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is consistent with what I saw with my own eyes, though I heard reports from Mihailov and from Major Dudley that there had -- or that people within the town had told them of occasions when people had been forced to do things that they had not wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the quote from your statement in Galic: "Civilians in the enclaves who had taken up arms to defend themselves..." the question I'm going to ask you is partly as a French speaker and as a military officer, educated at Sandhurst and elsewhere, are you familiar with the expression "lever en masse"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That refers, does it not, to persons who, on the approach the enemy, spontaneously take up arms to resist the invading troops without having time to form themselves into armed units; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close. It's not entirely accurate, but it is good enough. Where it is not correct is that "lever en masse" means that they are called to arms, not spontaneously come to arms. "Lever" means raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now you told us yesterday that the Serbs had occupied 60 percent of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the war. So would you agree essentially they were invading troops on that territory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory that they occupied and forced the people who were living there, usually Bosniaks, sometimes Bosnian Croats out of the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So as a matter of military terminology, would you agree that Srebrenica's fighters, as far as you could tell, were lever en masse in this sense?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now regarding the tactical position in Srebrenica you told us you received about a third of your intelligence from Major Dudley.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, could the witness please be shown War Hospital, which is Exhibit D119, and it's pages 154 to 155. Have you -- are you familiar with that book by Sheri Fink?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's another book in which your name features, so you can add it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to your reading list. In fact I can read the passage in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Go ahead, Mr. Jones. Let's lose as little time as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's page -- starts at page 154, last paragraph. And it's referring to Dudley, in the enclave and around the time of late March 1993. It says, "Constantly shadowed by two Bosnian minders he has also mapped the perimeter of the enclave and attempted to understand what the Muslims and Serbs in this part of Bosnia are fighting about. He has concluded..." I will stop there so you have it. It's page 154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if we can put it on the ELMO, please, and then the witness can follow from the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the bottom paragraph of page 154 and going over to page 155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry, I think it will appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact it's going on to page 155. "He has concluded that the value of Srebrenica is eminently defendable and identified positions from which it can be protected. He explained to some key Bosnian soldiers that they should dig up the roads and block the trails leading into the town and set up defence in depth - forward positions with multiple fall back positions. This way the light infantry could fight off an armoured Serb attack. When the Bosnians argued they couldn't pull it off, he advised them to get out. The place is the Alamo, he thinks, it isn't going to last." The Alamo is part of military lore [Realtime transcript read in error "law"], isn't it? It's the last stand of a besieged --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mexico, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, "lore," rather than "law." Now, when you first arrived in Srebrenica, in fact there was a very large log or tree, wasn't there, placed across the road?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at Konjevic Polje. Not at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Do you agree with the assessment as set out by Major Dudley in that extract?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I -- in terms of the geography, yes, it was mountainous, hilly terrain and, in principle, it should be fairly easy to defend. The point he is not taking or did not appear to take into account is that you need weapons with which to do that and the -- and you need anti-tank weapons, particularly those 66 millimetre, and they had, I may have said they were gold dust, but there was just no way they had the weapons with which to mount a serious defence of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact the tactical position was worse for the Bosnians than described by Major Dudley?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You dealt a lot with General Morillon imploring Oric in March of 1993 to cease his offensives. My question is seeing the talk of the Alamo there, and your reports of Oric speaking of fighting in and among the houses and dying there with his people, do you maintain that Oric was doing anything other than waging a desperate defence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To fill out the picture of Srebrenica a little more, you told us about the hospital and a pile of human body parts; fingers toes, hands, limbs was on the hospital slope. Now you also spoke about this in your statement in Galic and you said -- and the reference is 02192833, page 26, first paragraph: "Larry Hollingsworth -- again -- UNHCR man -- later persuaded the town committee to get it cleared away." That's this pile of limbs. "As part of his efforts to shame them into cleaning up the town and improving hygiene. The problem was that most people believed the Bosnian Serbs were going to kill them and the only question was when. In these extraordinary circumstances, they had simply given up trying and normal attitudes to matters like hygiene, food, tidying up, cleanliness, et cetera, simply fell into disuse. What was the point? They already considered themselves the walking dead." Quite simply, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would add, in clarification, that that was very much for the -- that was the refugee situation. The situation for some of the original inhabitants of Srebrenica or people who had their own houses and so on was slightly better, but not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on the same page, concerning the water supply, you said, "Water came from the river that flowed through Srebrenica but was polluted with offal, human excrement, urine, washing water and oil." Now as far as you're aware, was that the water supply for most of Srebrenica's residents?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And a comparatively trivial matter in light of what we discussed, but you told us you took paper from your diary, I think, to light something?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To light fires, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that paper was also very scarce in Srebrenica when you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we have a number of documents to take you through now and to do it in an orderly way I will go through chronologically and for reasons which I won't get into we're going to need to go in and out of private session for that exercise. So in fact, we should probably go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And proceed with the caveat that if you are going to refer specifically to the document, in other words, it needs to be stated who is the author, what kind of a document it is. Then obviously we have to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I quote from the document without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Did you form the opinion, in Sarajevo, that the Serb policy was to blockade in eastern enclaves essentially to use starvation as a tool of war against the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now on the second page of this document, paragraph 3, we see reference to the following: "In close consultation with UNPROFOR, we decided to proceed with our obligations to provide urgent assistance to the destitute populations of Srebrenica, garage, and other locations in eastern Bosnia as one part of our overall distribution of aid to all those in need". Now as assistant to the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia, you worked with UNHCR in working out where aid was most needed.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In late 1992 the assessment was that aid - food and other essentials - was desperately needed in Srebrenica and the other enclaves; correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if this document could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It will be given an exhibit number immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Under seal too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But temporarily under seal, until we clear this matter up. What is the next number, is it D? 221, yes. So this will become Defence Exhibit 221. Thank you. It will be temporarily under seal, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will need to move into private session for the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Move into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, dealing now with your -- the briefing for your trip to Srebrenica, which comes next in time, you've told us how you had meetings with Mr. Lagumdzija and General Halilovic in which they mentioned to you that a Colonel Oric was, I don't know, their man in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Lagumdzija. Lagumdzija was the minister of refugee affairs. I can't recall us ever meeting Lagumdzija together with Halilovic. Lagumdzija we might have met with Ganic, or Lagumdzija on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact Lagumdzija at that time was vice-president of the government, wasn't he? He wasn't actually a minister for refugees. Or...

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, he had been minister of refugees earlier and continued to have to speak with General Morillon about refugee affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In any event so it is Halilovic who told you the commander in Srebrenica was Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either Halilovic or Ganic, who we met at the same time after meeting President Izetbegovic prior to going into Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you give us a rough or even precise date for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3rd or 4th of March. We met both of them, I think, on both days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If with the Usher's assistance, if the witness could be shown a Prosecution exhibit, P358. The ERN is 01754001 to 01754011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is an intercept which we haven't accepted as authentic, but it is a Prosecution exhibit and I put it to the witness in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless he proves to you that it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not exactly. I suppose if it is authentic certain consequences follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just to explain, this purports to be an intercept of conversations from the 24th of March, 1993, so nearly three weeks after your meeting with General Halilovic, and I would refer you to Page 5 of 6 in the English. It's under III, and I will read it into the record: "Sefer called Hasim [illegible] because he forgot to tell him something." "S" -- which is for Sefer -- "Listen please, I forgot. Do you have any information on Naser?" Then the answer is: "Sure, personal data," et cetera. "S: Uh-huh." The other person: "I do not have." S: "What is his last name?" The other person: "Oric." S: "Are you sure?" The other person: "Sure. Naser Oric." S: "He is probably the commander of the Municipal Staff there." The other person: "Yep." S: "Did he establish some kind of a brigade there or a unit?" The other person: "No. Not officially, as far as I know, not." It continues, obviously, but my question to you is this: Are you positive that Halilovic in fact used the word "Oric," that he knew Oric's last name and referred to Colonel Oric when you had meetings with him? Do you maintain that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintain that he said that Colonel Oric was his local commander and that -- the commander of Bosniak forces and that he would try to get in touch with him in order to ensure that we had safe passage into the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you went to Srebrenica, it was with the name Colonel Oric on your mind as the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. In fact, when we came across the tree obstacle that you commented on a little bit earlier, when we first reached the Bosniak front lines and we were halted by the Bosniak soldiers on the front line, we asked them: Can you tell Colonel Oric that General Morillon is here and he would like to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've looked in the new diary which was -- I'm going to refer to it as the new diary, in fact it is the one before in time which was disclosed to us yesterday, and searched in vain for any meeting in which there is a reference to General Halilovic telling you he would contact -- you should contact -- sorry, he would contact Colonel Oric. Do you agree that there is perhaps no such reference in your diary?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely possible. It was not a, an issue that was of -- considered of import. When we would go into an area, we would meet with whoever was the local commander. That his name was Oric was not particularly significant and was not something that the -- that I was concerned about or particularly worried about keeping a record of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, there is in the diary a meeting on the subject which is with Siber?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And while we're at it, are you aware that he was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Unusual in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it in fact so unusual, or wasn't the ABiH in fact proud of its multi-ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I say it was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You know Jovan Divjak as well, I suppose. You were aware --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: High ranking member of the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Serb?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the record, it was a high-ranking member of the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a page from that diary. In fact I have to get my copy in front of me and I don't know if it is possible to put a page from that in front of the witness. It's the -- it is actually Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a new disclosure, not the diary which we looked at so far. In fact I will present my copy. That's probably easiest. All right. We're putting that page on the ELMO and the reference R0170974 and you can see the heading "Srebrenica" at the top. This is a meeting of the 7th of February, 1993 with Siber among others. Could you read what is written under Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Srebrenica. Cease-fire implemented the day you tell me you are ready. Cease-fire for three days. After that meeting between local commanders under the chairmanship of UN military observers. When are you ready to order cease-fire? Best place is Tuzla. Idea was on ground on confrontation line. Will instruct local commander to be at - somewhere - tomorrow at 1200 hours. Then meeting Thursday 1200 hours somewhere on confrontation line. Siber will phone Rasik about frequency and call sign for contact to be made."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree there is a reference to a local commander but no reference to Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now we need to move into private session for the next exhibit on the same subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now do you remember being proofed by the Prosecution when you came to the Hague? By proofing I mean that you were --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you gave testimony here, on this occasion, last week.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now do you recall speaking of meeting Oric in Konjevic Polje, describing him as, among other things, "bearded and intense"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then I'm quoting from the notes we have, anyway: "Introduced himself as the commander of the Bosniak forces in Srebrenica (may have said eastern Bosnia)." May have said eastern Bosnia. Now, when you gave evidence on Monday, you said and I'm quoting: "Q. What did he say he was? "A. He said he was the commander of the Bosniak forces in Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina." I put it to you that you went from saying maybe that was how he introduced himself, but that your original -- your initial impression was what he only said he was the commander of the pocket. You testified all of a sudden you were clear and categorical that it was a much broader area, the whole of eastern Bosnia, that Oric commanded.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language eastern Bosnia, Srebrenica and Gorazde were used by many people intermixed. Some people, when they referred to eastern Bosnia, meant Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde. Others meant only Srebrenica, Zepa. I would not be able to be specific, to say absolutely categorically it was Srebrenica that was said, or eastern Bosnia. At various times, both were said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's my point really, that eastern Bosnia encompasses a lot more Srebrenica, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It includes Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many people's minds, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that at any point anyone told you that Oric was a commander of Gorazde as well?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unclear about that. In our minds, Zepa was the enclave of Kamenica, Cerska, Srebrenica, and Zepa formed one area, whereas Gorazde was definitely separate. Quite how -- whether the Bosniaks held contiguous territory from Zepa to Srebrenica at that time, we weren't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was going to come to that when we look at the map which you drew. You've heard the name Avdo Palic, have you not, who is the commander of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check my diary. I can't recall it now, sat here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in your note of 5th, 6th March you say, "Naser was commander of the Srebrenica pocket," rather than eastern Bosnia, I think it's correct to say.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sat here, that is what I would say after all of the meetings that I had, is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's my suggestion which I put to you is that with time, the impression which you at least are conveying of Colonel Oric in the situation there has gone from one in which you knew of a person who was a commander in a pocket, to a position where today you seem to be more confident in expressing the opinion that he was commander in a much more organised sense of a larger area. Now would you accept that the former is the case? It was an organised structure in Srebrenica, firstly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not maintain that -- would it be appropriate for me to, to explain what my beliefs were? I can't prove them, but I can say what my beliefs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to your beliefs --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- by another route. I wouldn't want to invite a general expression of beliefs just like that. Now, on the subject of your meeting with Naser Oric in Konjevic Polje, didn't Naser Oric also make requests of Morillon and the United Nations, in other words it wasn't just one way, including a cease-fire, including humanitarian aid, but most importantly a request for the UN to station peacekeepers on the access points over the Drina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did specifically request that. I believe it is in my diary and...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Basically to deploy UN monitors on the borders of the state, the sovereign state of RBH to prevent foreign aggression from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his concern because he had told us about forces, Serb forces coming across the Drina from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you accept General Morillon never made any serious attempt to address that request?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What General Morillon tried to address was step 1, which was to get UNMOs into the pocket. Where they would be stationed was step two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You agree, do you, from what you knew of that period and from what you have told us of the Serbs calling the shots, they never would have countenanced United Nations observers on bridges into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never tested it, but your speculation I would share.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, skipping ahead for a moment, as we discussed, General Morillon was in Konjevic Polje. After he left there were shellings and people were killed and injured. When your party were in Srebrenica, women among others blocked your path so you couldn't leave. That's been presented during your examination-in-chief as a hostage scenario. I want to put a different scenario to you, which is that the people in Srebrenica, women and displaced persons, had heard of Morillon's comments broadcast around the world about Cerska, that he had -- that he had been there and that he hadn't smelt the odour of death. And that they were revolted by that. And they feared that Morillon would also downplay the appalling situation in Srebrenica. Is that something, firstly, which you would accept?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very surprised if any of the refugees in Srebrenica had had access to any radios and indeed any communication whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you accept, though, that because their lives depended on it in a way, they tried to keep him there long enough so that he would broadcast to the world the reality of the situation in Srebrenica, which the world did not know about and which the Serbs didn't want the world to know about, so that that would then be broadcast and people would know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Once he made the broadcast, or made the broadcast as you described, isn't it true he in fact he and your team were free to move around the enclave and in fact free to leave, after a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the point was always made that we had to leave someone in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you accept that your captivity lasted for, say, no more than say 24 hours, if that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I would be reluctant to call it captivity. I would call it "very strongly encouraged to stay in one place." For example, our weapons were never taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've seen in Larry Hollingsworth's book the reference to semantics. Would you have done the same as these women if you had been in their position?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to the document which we saw a moment ago which was given an exhibit number, and I don't think we need to go into private session, and I will quote from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If in the interpretation there is reference to the source of that document, then obviously we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. There is no reference to the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. It is -- well, to a certain extent there is a reference to the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's play it safe. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But later you said on the 17th of March, that Oric was deeply depressed and downcast.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the military situation in the enclave was deteriorating all the time, wasn't it, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the situation was even worse on the 21st of March 1993, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was getting worse every day. Serb attacks were continuing relentlessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that it was at the meeting on the 17th of March, 1993 - correct me if I'm wrong - that Oric said something about his men going beyond what was necessary and you said "killing ten people when five people would do."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First, this was translated from Serbo-Croatian, wasn't it, so you don't know --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was Mihailov who was doing the translating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you don't know the exact words that were used.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it follows from that, doesn't it, you don't know whether he said, when he said "his men," whether maybe he said "his people" went beyond what's necessary, or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think he was talking -- because he tended to refer to "my people" rather than "my men," as in the English meaning of men as in men, military soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The "my people" could refer to Bosniaks firstly?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it could include civilians?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nor do you know, do you, whether when he was talking about 10 people being killed, whether that referred to Serb soldiers being killed as opposed to five Serb soldiers, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Serbs. I specifically remember thinking at that time does he mean soldiers, does he mean civilians? I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you said that he had said "sadly," sadly this occurred.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I take it at the time -- even at this time when there was the appalling offensive going on, he expressed regret at the loss of Serb lives.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was not -- his whole demeanour was one of -- he wished it were otherwise, and one of regret.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally on this subject, as a military man, would you agree -- you referred to discussion of the impracticality of taking prisoners, that doesn't necessarily mean that every one of the enemy gets killed, you can leave them an escape route, for example, if you can't take prisoners.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that that is what was done in Kravica in the attack on the 7th of January, 1993? That an access was left for the Serbs to flee towards the Drina?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge or no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the 21st of March, 1993 and the hand-over of the Serb prisoner, I just have one more clarification really on that. I asked you yesterday about the presence of any members of the war committee. I said,"Did you see any members present?" and you said "No." May I take it from that that you don't --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot remember. They may have been present. I can't confirm one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was the clarification I sought. Thank you. Now a couple of final matters before the break. You were interviewed by the Prosecution in relation to this case in late 2002, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was for the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When were you first interviewed by the Prosecution in relation to this case, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2002. Yes, I think so. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now, was that the first time you told anyone -- it just turned out that way -- that it had been Oric whom you saw, whom you say you saw on that day, the 21st of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it's the first time I told anyone involved with this court. I'd had no reason to talk about that. I had certainly mentioned it, as I did many other things that had happened in Bosnia, to -- in previous years, in conversation with former colleagues, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you referred to this, you were consulting your recollection, rather than anything you wrote down contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just dealing with being interviewed by the Prosecution, that was nearly a decade after events, correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. It is slightly early but we have a technical issue, which is -- I want to show a video and because this is an e-court, it makes it more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't ask me how it works. I do have an indication because I did the course, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can solve it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is pretty easy and it's actually easier than in the other booths -- other courtrooms. So we will have a break. 25 minutes, to be on the safe side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the record, you confirmed my name as lead counsel for the Prosecution. Not only I share this bench, also Miss Sanja Bokulic is here, next to our case manager. She's assistant case manager, and on short term project as whenever needed for acting case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information, Mr. Wubben. Yes, Mr. Jones. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just before the break, we were dealing with the 21st of March again, briefly, 1993. Now, said that the person you saw step out of the Mercedes was swaggering. Would it be right to say that is not consistent with the behaviour of Oric which you had seen before then?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was extremely surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did part of your surprise come from the fact that, that he had been downcast the last time you had seen him and the situation certainly hadn't improved since then?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, for a variety of purposes, we want to show a little video clip but part of it is to observe the demeanour of Naser Oric. And by way of introduction, the video we're going to show, it's P427 we're going to show an extract of. And it's of Konjevic Polje on the 6th of March, and so we will also see some of the people, hopefully, in the video, possibly including yourself. That remains to be verified. And the starting point, we're going to start at 30, so, yes, if the video could be played, please. And we want to check, of course, that the witness can see. There is no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have an image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I now do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Okay, we can just play it and -- now, that's the APC of the British soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know who that tall man in the foreground is? Can you stop for a second.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the blue UN helmet?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: His back to us.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His back? Not entirely sure. I see what -- actually, he has his back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right -- is -- I'm not saying that that is Major Alan Abraham, but there was a tall --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Alan Abraham was a tall -- a tall British major. He was the commander of the unit whose armoured vehicles we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: His nickname was "The Draft," I believe?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, but it does not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person sitting there on the APC as a Mr. -- major, or captain at the time, Sterrenberg [phoen]; do you know --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name, but the picture is not distinct enough for me to be able to confirm that that is who I remember it as.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will play on, if you recognise anyone as we go along, then please say.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My screen is blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will you pause. Right. That's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From when you spoke, I did not see any -- any pictures. I now have a still.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We can carry on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise that as obviously Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mihailov.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's you, isn't it, there, indicating?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's myself on the right. And that's Mihailov behind Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this is Morillon meeting with the people in Konjevic Polje on the 6th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person who General Morillon is speaking to?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would the name Senso Sahilovic [phoen] mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm just going to play this a bit longer because I want to ask if you recognise this gentleman who has just come into the screen with a yellow hood.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Bottom right. Of course his back is to us, but I --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- I suggest it is our client, Naser Oric. And we can establish that from other sections of this video, but if you --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's got -- he's got the beard, certainly, that he had, that I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Part of the reason why I'm asking you to look at this clip, is that -- there we go --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is more like it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that, would you agree, in this scene, there is no prima donna-ism, if I can put it that way, on his part, he is simply standing there behind other people, listening to what is going on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then that's the --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's him departing from Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that Major Sterrenberg on the right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean getting into the vehicle or do you mean in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the camouflage.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the camouflage? I would need to rewind the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not terribly important.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mihailov looking straight at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can stop the video there. Now, at the first meeting with Naser Oric in Konjevic Polje, there were men there whom you said you could tell from what they said and from their body language, that they were, subordinates of Oric or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, obviously you couldn't understand what was said, could you, because you didn't understand --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could never understand what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm obviously not going to ask you to reenact the body language from which you inferred this relationship, but I take it they weren't fawning or bowing to Oric or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To me, it seemed, if you will pardon my expression, a very professional set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you accept that inferences about superior-subordinate relationships based on body language is somewhat flimsy?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say they're flimsy. I would say that they were proper. I mean, when I say there was a superior-subordinate relationship, it was an entirely proper relationship. There wasn't any threatening or angry shouting. But it was -- it was profession -- it looked professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And I take it you would accept that any inferences about superior-subordinate relationships based on body language would be confined simply to those half a dozen individuals that --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now just a couple of more questions on the topic of your first arrival in Srebrenica. You said that the people, the authorities in Sarajevo said they would contact the people in Srebrenica to alert them of your arrival. Isn't it also true that Mihailov, as you drove slowly into the enclave was shouting and waving a UN flag?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it true that that could very easily alert the local fighters to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the whole intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said that the people you met were, I think you said were Oric's men because they took you to him. I put it to you that actually the most you can say, from those observations, is that you were met by some people who took you to Oric. Not that they were his men, necessarily.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned we would turn back to this map with the lines that you drew. Did you personally draw the lines?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So if the witness could be shown P511, which is the map. And while that is being --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew those lines on Sunday. In other words, a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your evidence was that this map represents the position in terms of confrontation lines, et cetera, in early February 1993.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It represents what our belief was. Whether it was accurate is, of course, a different issue, because we didn't have troops -- UN troops on the ground with which to confirm one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well I'm going to suggest to you a number of ways in which it is inaccurate and it is not a criticism, obviously, but it is to have an accurate map. If it could be placed on the ELMO, it is probably easiest. Actually, may I make a suggestion a belated suggestion. I folded the map in such a way that maybe it would be easier to put it on the ELMO. At any rate that is the way I would do it, which you have done already. Thank you. Now, firstly, this map does tend to suggest that at that time the enclaves of Zepa, Srebrenica, Cerska and Kamenica are all part of a contiguous Bosniak-held territory. I put it to you that that is simply wrong for a number of reasons. Firstly, if you see -- do you see Podravanje, almost exactly between Srebrenica and Zepa? There is a cross --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would suggest and you may or may not be able to help us with that, but there were Serb lines in the Jilay [phoen] -- you also see Jilay a bit further on - the Jilay-Podravno area.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Any Bosniak trying to walk between Zepa and Srebrenica ran a grave risk of being killed in a Serb ambush. Is that something you could help us with?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed that it was possible to walk between these places, but that there were patrols or forces from both sides who moved in the areas, and it was certainly not free passage, but behind a secure front line. That was our understanding at the time. And in fact, Murat Effendic, one of the things we asked him about was, just how did you move that? What is possible? And that was one of the things he described to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he describe it to you, though, as a dangerous passage?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, you would -- you were never quite sure who would appear around the next corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You see Milici, which on this map, following up from that road where we saw Podravanje, Jilay, Milici?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that that was a town which was completely in Serb hands in February 1993. Again, is that something which you can help us with, or do you maintain that it was Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't confirm whether it was or was not. The data points that we had were that Kamenica was in Bosniak hands, Cerska was in Bosniak hands, Zepa was in Bosniak hands, Srebrenica was in Bosniak hands. From the description of -- sorry, Konjevici we obviously knew was in Bosniak hands. And from descriptions that we had from people like Murat Effendic, from the mayor of Gorazde, et cetera, was that broadly speaking that was what was held. But what I have drawn here is based upon the main towns that I have just described to you. The fact that the line here goes this side of the village or that side, I cannot comment whether Milici was held by Bosniaks in the end of January then captured by the Serbs. I just don't know. It's not my -- not my ability to provide information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Well, on this map, as part of the key, you have a circled green as a significant location.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I take it, or may I take it from what you've said, that another way of seeing that is that those circles around Zepa, Srebrenica, Cerska, Kamenica, means that those areas were certainly in Bosniak hands?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But as for the rest of it, you really weren't so sure as to where confrontation -- confrontation lines went, where there were risks of ambushes by enemy forces and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would even -- whereas there was a confrontation line here, in other words a front line which was held and there were guards and so on, there was -- my understanding was there was no real confrontation line around Srebrenica. The only place where there was an analogous confrontation line was in this area here, between Bratunac and Potocari. There may have been elsewhere, but in all of these other areas there was no front line. There was just steeply -- steeply mound -- steeply wooded hills, mountains, and very small numbers of people. So anyone who wished to infiltrate in any direction could do so, probably at -- obviously at some risk, but there was no guarded front line, was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So as far as this map is concerned, when we see this thick red line going around Zepa, Srebrenica, Kamenica and Cerska, I take it then that we should not understand that to be a solid contiguous Bosniak territory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And in fact, just staying with that map for a moment, we see Osmace there, south of Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was mentioned, that location was mentioned in your diary a lot, wasn't it --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- in the context of shellings and bombings by --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The UNMOs went down from Srebrenica on quite a few occasions to observe what was going on in that area, and there quite few references in my diary that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, I would put it to you that Sase at this time too was in Serb hands even though it appears to be in Bosniak territory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, where is Sase?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sase is towards the east, towards the Drina from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may well be. Bear in mind that what I was trying to depict here was the beginning of February and whereas the time of my diary and my time in Srebrenica was obviously in March, by which time the Serb offensive had been going on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, with the Serb offensive the enclave shrunk to next to nothing in a matter of a few weeks, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It shrank, my understanding is, to literally just around here, by the 25th or so of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, on Gorazde, you depicted these dotted lines to suggest some movement between the Gorazde enclave, but I would suggest, and tell me if you agree, that Gorazde was a completely different enclave.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, indeed. By movement what I mean is nighttime infiltration, at risk. Not just walk up the high street. It's absolutely not the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If a few adventurous souls managed to clamber through the hills and get there.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very brave and courageous souls.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with this map, thank you very much for those clarifications. With the usher's assistance I would like to move to the next exhibit. My information is -- well there is no ERN number, certainly no R prefix, so we needn't go into closed session. This is a statement by Sadako Ogata the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a document which has been supplied to you by the Prosecution or is it a document that you acquired yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, you can see from the footer that it's in the public domain, available from the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. So we don't have any problems with this possibly being classified by Rule 70. So let's proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's a statement to the United Nations Security Council on the 11th of March, 1993. Now, page 2 and 3 of this document deal with the situation in Srebrenica. If I could just direct your attention to the last paragraph on page 2, firstly: "My biggest concern remains the government-held enclaves in Eastern Bosnia where access has not only been hampered and delayed but in many instances has been denied altogether. I've been increasingly disturbed by the prohibition of relief as a weapon of war, and of ethnic cleansing. The creation of yet another fait accompli." Now you've confirmed, haven't you, that your opinion was the Serbs were using starvation as a weapon of war against the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would simply ask for a defence exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be given defence exhibit number D215 -- 225. It will be kept in the record in the normal way. It is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, indeed. Sorry, we have another exhibit which is going to be passed up. This, too -- this has - I stand to be corrected by the Prosecution - it has an R prefix, but I received from the Prosecution a list or our list with "okays" next to various entries and I understand this one is one of the ones that has been cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you verify this, Mr. Di Fazio, please, because it is important, before we proceed. It's the document which has, as the last four digits, 46762, 6762.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it assists, I have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No problems with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can proceed in open session for this document, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I am obliged to my learned friends for that confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now this, firstly, is signed by Ronnie Denyft.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Denyft.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Denyft. I always have problems pronouncing his name. He was the Belgian UNMO.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was SMO North, senior military observer north, who was the senior UN military observer in the north-eastern section of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he was based in the hotel just north of Zvornik. He had a headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And this is -- it's undated but it must be between, I would suggest between the 14th and 17th of March, 1993. Because those dates appear?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that he left Srebrenica shortly after the General's declaration that he would stay and that he came back in again, into Srebrenica, a number of days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this is a special report on a situation in the Srebrenica area, signed by that gentleman. And the ERN is R004762 to R004761.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a regressive mode of numbering the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I have three questions on this document. Firstly, paragraph 7, if you see that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's a reference to UNMOs seeing airplanes from Serbia coming and bombing Muslim villages on the 13th of March, 1993. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the things we were talking about yesterday and you asked me about those entries in my diary where I had recorded those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then the general situation is set out in paragraph 10. This confirms, doesn't it, what you told us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, could we place it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. This paragraph, if you can have a look at it, confirms what you told us, that very large numbers of people were living out in the streets in temperatures of up to minus 20, burning plastic buckets for warmth.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you agree that in this document there is no mention of Naser Oric, firstly.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, because when Major Denyft left the pocket, we had not yet met Colonel Oric in Srebrenica itself. Our only meeting with him was the one at Konjevic Polje a number of days previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And in that paragraph, however, we do see the military commander tries to do something but he is helpless. And that was echoed in your diary entry at 3442, I think it was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Local commander appears helpless. Is that the same local military commander of the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that is who I was referring to and I assume that that must be who Major Denyft was referring to. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You don't recall that person's name?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask simply for an exhibit number for that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be given defence exhibit number D226.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now the next exhibit which we have -- in fact we understand it hasn't been cleared, so we need to move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can I see it first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
