utterances.text: It is R0046756. If it has been cleared in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I said I am going to see it first. In the meantime I expect Mr. Di Fazio to check properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's one of the problematical ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see why. Let's go into private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As long as you don't identify, from your reading the author of this -- if you mean to identify the author, obviously we need to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's one question and then we can move into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. So do -- you have authorisation to read the part that you meant to ask the witness about?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know we're in open session. Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can -- we're in open session and I am permitted to read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Provided you do not read beyond that in a manner which would expose or reveal the identity of the author of -- of that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the quote is: "here around me there are thousands of children in great danger of starving to death unless road and air convoys are able to get here." Now, is it right that that was a message sent out -- I won't say by whom, but by the person whom we've seen in the document on the 13th, I believe the 13th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that text is all in my note -- in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. So this would be a question of assigning an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered by the defence and is being admitted and marked as Defence exhibit D227.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour. I just have a few more exhibits to tender. With the Usher's assistance, the next exhibit, again, has no "R" prefix so I assume it's -- it's okay. It's a document from the headquarters, Bosnia command, of 18th of March, 1993. Firstly, this was sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before we proceed. Mr. Di Fazio, since this is not any different from some of the other documents that were classified or covered with confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please check?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just give me a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise to you, Mr. Jones. Before we proceed, I think we need to clear this. Incidentally, while Mr. Di Fazio is checking, making his verifications, the previous document D227 will be kept under seal for the time being until we get the clearance to make it public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If it assists the Prosecution I can provide information that this was received 23 -- received by us on the 17th of December, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's correct. I think that that's the bunch that is causing us these difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you to verify, Mr. Di Fazio, first of all, because I think it is my responsibility to make -- to ensure that rule 77 is observed. And, secondly, because if you have a glance at the B/C/S translation of the document, at the top-right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see, clearly, an "R" right in front of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it that that document also is covered by the confidentiality bond that is covered by rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. I don't think there is any doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think too, but it is my duty to raise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I suggest that we go into private session while we deal with this document and we will, of course, make the same enquiry with respect to this one that we will in respect of all of the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's the safe course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So all right, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Jones, did you get the message?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I did. I will be able to deal with this document briefly, but I wonder, I might mention at this moment, that the next document has the ERN R0122481 and my information is that that has been cleared but it seems worth it to mention that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you have mentioned it, I think the Prosecution team can verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can. That's cleared, but it's just this one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This one isn't as yet. So let's go into private session again for a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In that meeting with General Morillon and Naser Oric, didn't he in fact, on this same theme, talk not just about fighting to the bitter end but of dying with his people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He talked of many things. In fact, that meeting was, to the day, 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have we given an exhibit number to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't as yet, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At that meeting then, 12 years ago to the day, Naser Oric had resigned himself to dying in the near future?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not somebody who gave the impression of someone who would give up. He never gave us the impression that he thought he was going to die. He was always going to keep going, keep trying. I think you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, yes, I will ask for an exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, which will be kept under seal for the time being is being tendered as a defence document and is being marked as D228.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the next document we've received the information just now that that is okay and has been cleared, it's a fax from Mr. Leentjes of the 20th of March, 1993. The ERN is R0122481 to R0122484. I would ask you to look at the assessment. First, I will just read paragraph 8 into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you put the document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, may I ask you, the markings on this page, both on the left -- to the left and to the right of paragraphs 8 and 9, are those in the original or are those your work?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They're not our work. That's been in the document as we received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's in mine as well, if Your Honours please. I can't tell you who made those markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 8, and this is, is it not, the 20th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date, time group is 20, 2355, Alfa March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So: "The Serb attack on the Srebrenica enclave continues unabated. Despite the recent success of General Morillon to get the relief convoy into Srebrenica, the Serbs seem intent to continue this offensive as part of a general aim to continue to capture areas which can be taken at little cost. Currently, the Serbs are clearing up to four to five villages per day. They have received a lot of support from across the border in Serbia during this offensive. The Serbians have supported the BSA, Bosnian Serb army, with artillery fire, aircraft bombers and ammunition resupply convoys, as well as having allowed the Serbs to stage from within Serbian borders to attack from the east and south of the enclave." As far as your intelligence was concerned at the time, does that accurately describe the military situation on that day?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is entirely accurate, as far as I'm aware. The only one that I cannot comment on is the and ammunition resupply convoys. I had no information specifically of that specific element, but all the rest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Then paragraph 9 deals with the refugee situation. And I will quote that: "This offensive is creating a refugee situation of huge proportions. The number of refugees in the Srebrenica enclave is assessed to be around 80.000. It is estimated that there are 20.000 refugees in Srebrenica alone, and an additional 20.000 in Zepa. The condition of many of the refugees is very poor. There are an estimated 200 seriously wounded and an additional 100 less seriously wounded. A death rate of 20 persons per day is reported. The pending massive medevac to Tuzla or any other single location would create a severe problem because of overcrowding in the city hospital there."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I am being asked to intervene and ask you to please slow down when you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Does that accurately describe the refugee crisis as it was on that day? The 20th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the numbers that Larry Hollingsworth had reported and that are in my diary. The only thing that I cannot comment about is the difficulties of overcrowding at the Tuzla hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact whose assessment was this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was headquarters, Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Kiseljak's assessment. Colonel Leentjes would have drafted it. However it would have been authorised by General Cordy-Simpson, in other words it was the headquarters' collective assessment taking information from myself, which I was providing over the radio, together with information that they gained from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move on to the next page, paragraphs 10 and 11. I will read them as slowly as I can. Paragraph 10 firstly. "If Srebrenica falls then the refugees have little option but to move south towards Zepa. As pressure from the diminishing enclave to the north increases, refugees would then see Gorazde as their final haven. The route there is a very tenuous corridor. It is a route used only in extremis and only by fit persons. Of those refugees who attempt the journey, only the very strongest would survive. The Serbs anyway are unlikely to allowed unhindered passage to Gorazde as this enclave would then represent a threat to the Serbs given its recent influx of refugees. Moreover, refugees would arrive in Gorazde only to find conditions already becoming quite harsh there also." Now firstly, what is said about the journey to Gorazde is consistent with what you told us in relation to the map just now?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you share, at the time, this very pessimistic forecast of what is likely to happen if Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an assessment which is produced outside of my knowledge. My own view, at that time, and my own view now, is that it would be entirely unrealistic for refugees to be able to move from Srebrenica to Zepa or Gorazde because refugees had been flooding in the opposite direction into Srebrenica. For them to go back that way, they would run straight into the Serbs who were attacking out behind them. I think that Colonel Leentjes when he wrote that was not entirely away quite how far the Serb front lines had advanced and I would -- I personally believe it's entirely incredible that any refugees at all could have reached Zepa or Gorazde from Srebrenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It would have been a journey of several days to Zepa, correct, at that time, which only the fittest could --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is if the Serbs had even allowed it to pass, and I don't believe they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now the next paragraph, 11, finally. "If free passage (with transport) cannot be arranged for the refugees in the Srebrenica pocket within the next 7 to 14 days, indications are that the Serbs will carry out a genocidal 'cleansing' of the entire enclave, resulting in the potential death of up to 80.000 human beings. In any case, there is little hope that current efforts to get the Serbs to halt their attack will be successful. They are unlikely to stop this offensive until the enclave is cleared one way or another." Isn't it right, firstly, that even then -- this is -- we all know what happened in July of 1995. This is 20 March, 1993. But there were warnings then if Srebrenica fell the result would be genocide, i.e. huge massacres of the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our nightmare as well and the reason -- the indications, that came from the statements by the Serbs that they were going to sort out the - I use "sort out" in inverted commas - the -- what they called war criminals in the Srebrenica pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the Bosniak expression "kad-tad," or at least rather than in Serbian, "kad-tad," meaning one day we'll get our moment to recover --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in the way you just described it. Because I wasn't following the Serbo-Croat in conversations. What I did pick up time and time again from Mihailov was revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would like to ask for an exhibit number if it hasn't been given yet to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No it hasn't been given an exhibit document yet, Mr. Jones. This document is being tendered and admitted and it will become Defence Exhibit D229.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. In that regard I would like to read what appears in your statement in the Galic case. And when speaking about the Serb attacks in the enclave, gobbling up village by village, as you described it, you said, and the reference is page 24 of that statement of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your assessment, Mr. Jones, whether the witness ought to be given a copy of his statement or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if there is going to be any lengthy reference to his statement, I suggest that he be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It is simply one sentence and, if the witness agrees with that sentence, then I won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at any time, Colonel, if you would like to have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the ERN is 02192831, and it says: "The impression generated amongst the civilian population was of a relentless unstoppable momentum that could only end with eventual death of everyone inside the enclave."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my -- that is correct and that is my belief as to what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you also confirm from what you gathered from conversations with people in Srebrenica, that at that time, March 1993, they were looking to Naser Oric as a sort of legend, as he's been described, to save them from that appalling fate, if possible, if anyone could.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to place this in the context of the situation. The people there, particularly the refugees, they believed they were going to die. As I've described previously, it was not a question of "if," it was only a question of when. Against that background, yes, there was this hero, Naser Oric, but he had very few weapons, he had very few soldiers. The Serbs had many weapons, the Serbs had many soldiers. They didn't believe that he would actually be able to help them and defend them. But they believed that he was doing his best.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, would you agree, that -- well, you've described Oric as the commander of this pocket, as being responsible for all of these people in one form or another. The 27-year-old commander, that is a huge responsibility to bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours please, it's not a quibbling matter, and the evidence of the witness, as I've understood it thus far, is that he was the military commander in the area and I think the witness has been at pains to make a distinction between civilian authorities and military authorities. Now, I have no problem, of course, with Mr. Jones eliciting evidence of the image of the defendant during that time, of course I have no problem with that, but we've got to be precise about what the witness has said about the position of Mr. -- of Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond? I'm happy to confine it to military matters. We agree that the evidence is only that he was responsible for military matters. I can simply -- I can put it much more simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except when you try to direct the witness to distinguish between saying "my men" and "my people." But I suggest that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you try to restrict your questions to the military aspect or the military role that your client was fulfilling at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest is a perfectly legitimate question and please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you confine your answer to the military aspects. As a military commander, with this appalling possibility of the lines falling, the town falling, and ensuing massacre, do you agree as a decorated military man, that this is a terrible burden for a commander, certainly a young commander to bear?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was operating in the most adverse and most difficult of circumstances and I cannot imagine having to operate in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You agree that would exert a terrible psychological pressure on someone, from your military experience, to be in that situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally on this matter, in it's opening speech, the Prosecution described Naser Oric as "a warlord drunk with power." Is that how Naser Oric struck you in your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not how he occurred to us on the -- on any occasion, other than that one occasion on the 21st, around the hand-over of the prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would that behavior, to the extent that if it was indeed Naser Oric, in your opinion, could that be explained by the appalling psychological pressure?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not in a position to sit in judgement over such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he is qualified either to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is really based on his observation, but that's fine, Your Honour. I believe we've given an exhibit number, have we, to the last document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I lost track. So we have another exhibit now, which again there is no R prefix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see it before. I want to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is a document from -- well, perhaps I won't mention the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I better see it first because I want to make sure. Was this document given to you by the Prosecution, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was provided to us by the author. By the source. And he didn't place any restrictions on its use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is not a document that was provided to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you think that when it was given to you it was covered with -- by confidentiality, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from Dr. Simon Mardell of the World Health Organisation, dated the 12th of April, 1993. Now, you obviously met Dr. Simon Mardell?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're familiar with his, I will put it, very adventurous or daring act of volunteering to walk into the enclave from Konjevic Polje to see the situation in Srebrenica on your first visit to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a brave and committed man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you also describe him as reliable and measured?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this report is about the appalling, I would suggest appalling shelling suffered by Srebrenica on the 12th of April 1993. Again, this is after you left the enclave, but there is a reason why I will be putting this to you. I will just read from the beginning: "Subject: Slaughter of civilians in Srebrenica. The sitreps of Louie Gentille today at 1654 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "The sitreps of Louie Gentille today at 1654 and 1911 hours describe appalling casualties from shelling of the densely packed town of Srebrenica. If in his earlier report he is forced to use the phrase 'after a day of terror and horror,' we can only guess at the scenes later which have led to a total of 56 dead and 73 seriously wounded." Then further on he says: "With a population of around 60.000, many of whom are displaced from what has previously been acknowledged as ethnic cleansing, then the present situation can only be described as an impending Holocaust." Then in the next paragraph he cautions, in a sense, the Serbian people of what will follow if a genocide is perpetrated by their leaders. Do you see all of that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're familiar with this -- this shelling on the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read about it in the -- in the media. And Louie Gentille is a UNHCR officer from the UNHCR Belgrade office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, in the chapter from Larry Hollingsworth's book at pages 215 to 216, he expresses in his hottest-part-of-hell speech a similar sentiment to the one which you expressed for General Mladic in his case for the army commander who ordered that shelling.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you agree from this document that Dr. Mardell, too, appears to have feared in April 1993 that the Serbs would carry out a genocide in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment about this document, as it was in April. However when I spoke with Dr. Simon Mardell in Srebrenica around the 11th, 12th, 13th March, his opinions of -- then were the opinions which are reflected in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would it be fair to summarise the situation thus emerging from these documents and from your intelligence, that the Bosniaks in Srebrenica were and knew they were surrounded by deadly foe who could easily reap death and destruction and was willing to do so?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they fully expected him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Defence Exhibit D230.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have just a few more exhibits now. The next one, again, there is no "R" preface, but again perhaps Your Honour would like to see the document first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have the same problem that we encountered earlier on. It's true that in the English version there is no "R" number, but in the B/C/S translation thereof, there is. So unless Mr. Di Fazio announces that confidentiality has been lifted, we will need to treat this document as we did with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, registrar. We are in open session, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it also the case though that your radios were more modern, more reliable, more secure, and in a great many ways far superior to the equipment which you saw in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The equipment in the PTT building was more reliable and was -- seemed to have better quality sound than the HF radios that we used. The TACSAT radio was secure but it was very difficult to use because you had to get up high on the mountain in order to be able to get a shot on the satellite.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that the radio in the PTT building was only as reliable as the generator --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- tied to the stream --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- which kept it going?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The comment a few days ago about the power of that radio, if it had had full power -- full, normal electricity, that was a very powerful, far, far more powerful than anything we had in our vehicles. Their issue was they had very little electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now going back to this, firstly, just on Major Dudley, did you find, from your dealings with him, that he was generally a reliable source of intelligence when you had opportunity to have independent verification?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He seemed reliable. He was -- no, I won't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can deal with this document quite shortly. As far as your report was concerned, isn't it right, from this, that on the 22nd of March -- on the 22nd of March, 1993, you were reporting a relentless Serb attack on the south-east of the pocket?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That information came from Major Dudley. It came from the UNMOs - that's the Osmace direction - and it was reported to us by Colonel Oric and it was reported to us by the members of the War Presidency. We had no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us, I think yesterday, that it was on an occasion of a meeting with the Serb commander that you saw, in his office when the offensive started, and that was early February 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct that was Major Pandurevic's office, who -- Major Pandurevic is, in my view, of some considerable note. He seemed to be General Mladic's right-hand man, in the area. And I described previously that Mladic seemed to push Gvero forward instead of himself. If we wanted to really know what Mladic was up to and wanted, it was: What was Pandurevic doing. And in his office, there was this -- I wasn't sure whether it was a tactical situation map or whether it was the plan, but it showed the front line from the Serb perspective every two days or so, starting from the 7th of February. And the deduction drawn from that was that it was a record, or the plan, for the successive offensive against the enclave to capture the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when one is dealing with this offensive in early 199 -- February, is it correct that it started - as far as you understand, as far as you are able to gather - at the beginning of February 1993 and it went right up to mid-April 1993 with the demilitarisation of the enclave; i.e., two months?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And the indication from that map - but I have no other source of confirming - was that the Serbs started that attack and planned it to start on the 7th of April -- 7th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You didn't ask Major Pandurevic about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When he came back into the office, he saw that the map was on the wall and he quickly pulled the curtain over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could have an exhibit number, please, for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D231.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we have another exhibit, which I think we need -- we need to go through the same exercise again. There is no ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see it first to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's exactly the same story as for the last document --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- provided to us by the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session. There is no indication, because I don't have the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think Mr. Jones said it was provided by the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't think we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it's from someone other than us, there is nothing we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we don't need to go into private session for this. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Right. So if you could look at this document. And firstly I would ask whether you agree that the date as stated there, 23rd of February, 1993, in light of the fact that it deals with a summary of the visit of 5 - 12 March 1993 is probably wrong.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the main thing is it is a summary of that visit by Dr. Simon Mardell to Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could only have provided this report after having been in Srebrenica having walked into there from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now, this is obviously a detailed report on the condition of the medical facilities and the public health situation as seen by Dr. Mardell in Srebrenica in March 1993. Firstly, I would ask you to look at page 3, medical conditions in the villages around Srebrenica. Second paragraph: "Many of the villages have lice as well as scabies. Some patients are dying from pneumonia and dysentery." I would simply ask you this: Were you aware, from your time in Srebrenica, of a general problem of lice infestation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. It had been mentioned by a number of people. Larry Hollingsworth also mentioned it. In fact, it's mentioned in his Merry Christmas, Mr. Larry as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That follows basically, doesn't it, from a mass of unwashed bodies in close proximity. That's what happens.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely to be expected, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I would also draw your attention to the following, on page 5. It's paragraph 3, displaced people, it's a reference to different groups of people. The bit which I am going to ask you about is the section which reads: "This group of people exists on food they beg from neighbours or steal from Serbian farms. Some families had members shot while attempting the latter." It's simply this: Are you aware, from your conversations with people in Srebrenica, that Serbs were shooting displaced persons, Bosniaks, when they went to try and steal food from Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no knowledge of -- I've certainly not heard anywhere of displaced people going and stealing food from Serbs. It would have been very foolhardy for them to do so. But I have no information that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would just ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document will become Defence Exhibit D232.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would Your Honours bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. We have 'til 12:30, don't we, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I can probably conclude before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There are just a few final matters which I need to tie up with, so if I am skipping around, you'll know why. On the radio, again, in the PTT building, as far as you were concerned, that was under the control of the war committee, wasn't it, or the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. In your prior statement, I believe it's in Galic, you refer to the "propaganda machines of the Bosnian Serb side." Were you -- first of all that's -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're aware - you were aware, weren't you, of a whole propaganda war that was being waged at the same time as the military conflict?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you heard or you referred to a story which you heard from the Serbs that Bosniaks had actually captured part of the Serb territory; i.e. --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that that was a complete fabrication?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible. It was simply reported in the international media and we had no means of corroborating it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the same would apply, wouldn't it, to claims by Dr. Karadzic, Mladic and others that from late January until March - I can't remember the exact figure, but it was thousands of Serb civilians killed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a number they kept on referring to and it was either 1.260 or 1.360. It's in my diary somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you form the opinion or have reason to believe that that was part of the propaganda war, those sorts of allegations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believed it was entirely possible. We had no, no means of corroborating that one way or the other. The only thing that we did know was that there was a grave of about 50 people south of Zvornik which was dug up. We were shown photographs of that, and SMO North in fact, Major Denyft was taken there. Though, who was in it, as in the -- where the bodies came from and who had put them, I was not in a position to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "entirely possible," I take it you mean it was entirely possible it was part of the propaganda war?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were not in a position to know what the truth was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right in your prior statement in the Galic case, I believe that you stated that it was Serbian soldiers who were in that grave. Is that right, that that is something which you --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have two final exhibits -- or actually, no, four final exhibits. The first two are completely open sources. It's the report by the United Nations into the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's extremely relevant, Your Honour. I will explain in a few words, if Your Honour wishes. In July 1995 -- we know the events of 1995. The United Nations later commissioned a report into the events, and that report looked into the whole -- the whole history of the enclave and of the propaganda campaign by the Serbs which I've referred to, and the reason I want to get into this area is that I think it is perfectly relevant and useful to Your Honours to know that there was constantly the use of the pretext of raids from inside the enclave as an excuse to prosecute the war effort by the Serbs. I want to put to this witness that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead. Go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there are two documents. Just to explain: One is a report on the report by the United Nations correspondent, Washington file. The other is the actual report itself. I want to start just with one Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paragraph from the report. It's paragraph 479. And I quote: "Serbs repeatedly exaggerated the extent of the raids out of Srebrenica --" "The Serbs repeatedly exaggerated extent of the raids out of Srebrenica as a pretext for the prosecution of a central war aim to create a geographically contiguous and ethnically pure territory along the Drina while freeing up their troops to fight in other parts of the country. The extent to which this pretext was accepted at face value by international actors and observers reflected the prism of moral equivalency through which the conflict in Bosnia was viewed by too many for too long." My first question is, going back -- and we're dealing with early 1993, was your intelligence or was your understanding that Serbs wished to eliminate the enclave so they could free up their troops elsewhere for use elsewhere in the country?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our opinion that the Serbs desperately wanted to free up troops because one thing, the one thing that the Bosniaks had was overall numerical superiority and they had very, very long extended front lines, confrontation lines. And they wished to free up -- or we believed that the Serbs wished to free up the troops who were surrounding the enclave in order to be able to redeploy those to other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you agree that this statement there about pretexts used by the Serbs could equally apply to late 1992, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that we were in negotiations with all sides to that conflict for many months and pretexts were used all the time. We can observe that the vehemence and the anger with which the pretext around Srebrenica were voiced - not by one or two people only but by most of the Serbs we came in contact with - was of a different -- it was more -- it was more angry. There is a difference. Now, why there was a difference we were not in a position to be able to confirm. We could certainly conceive of a number of military reasons why they would want to clear the enclave. The one you mentioned, shortening their lines, is one. Secondly, to prevent the continuous attacks that were occurring on their road from Zvornik down through Han Pijesak to Pale and Sarajevo is a -- is a second one. Sorry, is a second military reason that we -- that the Serbs told us that that was one of the things that they were very concerned about, as I gave in previous evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, you were an international actor in this -- on this scene and this is perhaps a personal question. But do you feel that in your dealings you were guilty of viewing the conflict through a prism of moral equivalency which was inappropriate in retrospect to the situation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were we there to try and save lives or to make political statements? We tried to save lives and certainly I took that my task both moral and the orders given to me by my government and passed through the Security Council, were to try and save lives. I was not in the game of making neither General Morillon, in the game of making political statements or supporting any political statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree, and this relates to passage in the other exhibit, that you were peacekeepers in a situation where there was a peace to keep?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were under Section 6 of the UN Charter, not Section 7. You're aware of the difference, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. Chapter or section?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Peacekeeping versus action by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. This Tribunal is a peacekeeping measure under Section 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Do you want to tender this document, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which is an extract from the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to General Assembly Resolution 53/35 of 1998, Srebrenica Report, to wit: Paragraph 479 thereof, is being tendered by the Defence and is being admitted and marked as Defence Exhibit D232. -- Sorry, 233.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in this regard, I would like you to quickly what I'm calling your new diary, the one you disclosed to us -- I'll pass the page up. It's R017 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What about the other five pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, I was treating them jointly. I would ask for an exhibit number for that as well. I asked a question which related to page 2 of 5, which refers to keeping the peace where there is no peace to keep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know you did. So this other document which is a -- is it an article, this? I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: An article authored by Judy Aita, with the Washington file, United Nations -- Washington file, United Nations correspondent. And which refers to the report on Srebrenica United Nations fate and its failure to control evil. And apparently dated 11th of -- 16th of November of 1999 and consisting of four pages, is being tendered and -- by the Defence and marked as Defence Exhibit D234.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Colonel, do you have your new diary, the diary which predates that diary in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The original is back at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask if it could be handed to the witness in this form simply because he might need to refer to earlier pages, but it is the highlighted section which I want to ask about and it is, as I say, R0170980, which is page 75. I think it refers to a meeting of the 8th of February 1993 in Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With Dr. Lukic, exactly. Is it right that General Morillon said to him, in relation to Serb obstruction to aid going to Srebrenica, "Your refusal to discuss aid to Srebrenica, et cetera shows that maybe those who criticised our mandate were right."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lukic was very hard line and completely inflexible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right that yourselves, you and General Morillon, were aware of criticisms of your mandate, even then?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very aware. It came up in just about every interview that journalists had with General Morillon from the end of October, 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that regard, if I could pass up the next exhibit, which is an extract from a book by Martin Bell called "In Harm's Way" and it is page -- pages 119 -- 191. My apologies are that there was some underlining which was by me because it was my copy and I didn't have time to find another copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honour's please I just wonder if Mr. Jones proposes to do anything with that diary entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the moment, I don't. For the simple reason I don't want to tender the whole diary because I haven't had the time to review its many pages. So I'm not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Jones' position. I'm not pressing for that but I just wanted to know what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't mention anything so I took it he didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you thank you. And yes, thank you, you can just return that to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There was mention the other day of philosophical issues of peacekeeping. I don't -- obviously this isn't the forum for that. But simply in relation to the criticisms of the mandate as set out in your diary, would that be reflected in the following passage which I will read -- page 190: "A Bosnian army officer dismissed it scornfully as a spoonful of aid so we can be healthier when we are hit by mortars and grenades. They wanted guns but were getting feta cheese, and Medecins Sans Frontieres asked: How can we think of passing food through the window while doing nothing to drive the murderer from the house? And then in fact the next sentence refers to General Morillon coining the phrase [French spoken] "angelisme." Do you recall General Morillon coining that phrase?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I remember he had a couple of meetings with Martin Bell and they discussed all of these sorts of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, further down there is Dr. Alain -- I'm not sure if I can pronounce his name, but the Secretary-General of Medecins Sans Frontieres: "Humanitarianism has served as an alibi for political impotence. It has never been further removed from what it asserts itself to be: a significant gesture of fraternity and hope. When the accounts are drawn up, when we finally know Bosnia's fate, humanitarianism will find itself sitting in the dock with the accused, a companion to the territorial conquest and ethnic cleansing, even to a certain extent making them possible." Would you agree that that is--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down for reading for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies yet again. Fortunately, I have finished my reading for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you say that that reflect the sort of criticisms which commentators were making of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects some of the criticisms. I have some opinions about them, but this is not for -- not the time or place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will become D235.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I notice it appears to have the autograph of Martin Bell. I can't recall whether he signed it or not, but I won't ask the witness to authenticate it even though it would make my copy even more valuable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, you hadn't mentioned it yourself but I think it should go into the record. You were in fact awarded the Military Cross, weren't you, for your time in Bosnia, including serving in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in particular the 20th of March at the yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You managed to prevent the Serbs crossing the bridge and entering the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when General Morillon went out to go and get the convoy and the Serbs took that as the yahoo moment: Now he's out of the way. Now we can go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have a final exhibit which is the supplement to the London Gazette, 12th of June, 1993. If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just if you can once you receive it, confirm it is the citation and that the matters referred to -- just for the record, really. That is the Military Cross, which is, is it, the second highest order of gallantry after the Victoria Cross?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for that to have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be Defence Exhibit D236.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. I think we will now have a 30 minute break. Do you have a long re-examination, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I was just about to ask -- address you about that. Not particularly long. There is a few issues that I need to raise. We will -- I think 20 minutes or 25 minutes or so. However -- however, I wonder if we could assume that we don't have to call any other witnesses today, because that will definitely eat into the second -- if Your Honours have questions as well, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- I don't think -- I think we need to talk sense, let's put it like that. Forget about another witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- after all this. He would walk in and walk out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's my point. So I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in any case, the next session has a maximum of 45 minutes of which you're taking 20 to 25. We will take another maybe five or ten and then we will call it a day. Thank you. --- Recess at 12.30 p.m. --- Upon resuming at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Colonel Tucker, the last exhibit that was given to you -- presented to you was D236. The publication in the London Gazette of the award of the Military Cross to you. And it says, a part of it says: "Every day Major Tucker would ensure that the main headquarters was debriefed and the necessary staff taskings were then able to be given. With such poor communications the whole of the United Nations command and control could easily have broken down without his total dedication." In order for you to ensure that the main headquarters was debriefed and that the necessary staff taskings were able to be given in a competent manner, was it necessary that your diary reflect as accurately as possible what you had seen, what you heard and what had been reported to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary was a means to an end. The end was the actual reports, of which the court has seen a number of copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. But my point is this: In order for your final reports to fulfil this task for which you received the award, your diary had to be, as far as you could make it, an honest and accurate reflection of what --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- information. Thank you. I just want to ask you some questions about the evidence that came out this morning, but perhaps before I get on to issues that arose this morning, while we're still on the topic of the diary, are you aware of your ever having made an inaccurate or dishonest note in your diary, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly occasions when I wrote in my diary information which was given at the time, which I subsequently found to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. That is one thing. I understand that. But your reporting of what was the information that was given to you, as far as you're aware, was accurate and honest, regardless of whether the source --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn to your evidence from today. You were asked questions about crowd control and it was suggested to you that it was impossible to control crowds or at least very, very difficult. Your answer was that it was perhaps possible with clear leadership. The means of crowd control, were they available in the sense of the presence of soldiers or police who were armed and able to marshal crowds, were those means present in Srebrenica while you were there?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, while I was there, I believe so, yes. What was lacking was the ability or the will to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And does that comment apply in respect of the starving and desperate refugees that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the soldiers. By soldiers, I mean people who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. You just told the Trial Chamber that you believe that the means of crowd control was there, available, namely soldiers who were armed. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers and policemen. I could not, by looking at them, tell the difference between a policeman and a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the means of crowd control. Just the means of crowd control. And that crowd control, is it your opinion, from what you saw and heard and observed, that means of crowd control could have been applied had the leadership been there, had the will been there, the determination been there to desperate people such as the starving refugees that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's more than just there, then, at that particular moment. It's if the refugees had been received and had been directed, to accomodation, if food had been distributed, if the refugees had been shown evidence of competence, they would have built up trust and it would have been much easier. It was more than just physically having people there then at that particular instant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked some questions regarding the pouch system for getting material out of the enclave. And you were asked some questions about the journalist Mr. Birtley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. The non-existence of a pouch system. I think that needs to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to misquote the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. And thank you for the observation, Mr. Jones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The absence of a pouch system. I think the thrust of your evidence would be, would it not, that there was no formal system in existence for getting documents and other material out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no formal system, but when requested, particularly by the journalists, we did everything in our power to try and facilitate, to make sure that that did get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. When you were crossing the lines of confrontation from Srebrenica into Serb --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. In Bratunac and crossing from one area into an area held by the opposing force, were you searched?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions we were searched. But that's two occasions out of 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what was the extent of the search on those two occasions? How intrusive of it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search on both occasions was a detailed search of the vehicle, but never a search -- never a body search. So they got everything out of the vehicle, put it out on the road, looked in every part of the vehicle, looked inside our backpacks and briefcases, but they never body searched us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked questions regarding the concept of lever en masse, and you agreed that -- I haven't got the precise evidence before me, but I think the thrust of it is that you agreed that it was a -- that it is a spontaneous taking up of arms in the face of an encroaching --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did not agree to that. In fact, he drew a distinction between spontaneous and the meaning of lever et cetera, and he explained the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry, would you be so kind as to reiterate your understanding.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point being that "lever" means "raise" as opposed to spontaneous call to arms. In other words, that there were people who were required to go and fight as opposed to just purely being volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did that situation apply, as far as you could see, in Srebrenica or not?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that that situation pertained in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were cross-examined at length regarding the notion of war crimes or allegations of war crimes on the part of the Serbs and its use as a pretext for -- basically for aggression and for refusal to negotiate. And you agreed that that was a pretext that was used in 1992 and 1993. Does that, in any way, affect your opinion or your -- I won't say opinion. Your evidence, both in examination-in-chief and again today, that there was an altogether different quality that you detected on the part of the Serb complaints regarding war crimes in that early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points. To start with, you said that I had agreed that the Serb complaints about war crimes were a pretext. I did not say that. What I said is that they could have been a pretext. I was not in a position to confirm one way or the other. The first point. The second one is that -- sorry. I must read back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a different quality, a greater anger, a greater fury on the side of the Serbs when they were referring to these allegations of attacks on unarmed civilians around the Srebrenica area. That did not mean that we were able to confirm whether or not they took place. What I can say is that the level of heat, excitement and anger was of a different level to that that's usually pertained when one side or the other was making accusations about the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked if the -- if it was a Serb war aim to eliminate the Srebrenica pocket in early February. And you answered that was your opinion, I think based on intelligence and -- well, I can't remember what it was based on but certainly you expressed the answer that it was your opinion. Had that been your opinion earlier in 1993 and in the latter part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had been our opinion that up until, broadly speaking, December, January -- sorry, December 1992, January 1993, the Serbs were content - I use the word advisedly - to leave the enclaves as they were and simply to -- and deny them food.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- I hope my note is accurate. I note that this morning, in cross-examination, you were asked about the idea of keeping peacekeepers on the Drina river, and I think you said that it was a suggestion by Colonel Oric at the Konjevic Polje meeting that peacekeepers be set up. Now, first of all, is my note correct? I think that's what you said this morning, isn't it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Can you recall how that topic arose, either on the 5th or 6th of March, at that first initial meeting with Colonel Oric?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Oric had reported that Serb forces had been crossing -- or forces had crossed from Serbia into Bosnia-Herzegovina by those routes, and when General Morillon was talking about the concept of deploying UN military observers in order to monitor a cease-fire, Colonel Oric made the point, amongst other places, they particularly need to be there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that a useful suggestion, from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a useful suggestion and a valid one. And had we been able to deploy UNMOs in sufficient numbers, that certainly is one of the things we would have tried to do, but it never got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Given that he made that suggestion, is it the case that he was fully engaged with you, willingly talking about the very idea of some sort of demilitarisation or cease-fire - I don't know which - involving peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that, whereas Colonel Oric was in favour of cease-fires, he was not and he absolutely rejected any notion of demilitarisation or disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was the suggestion of -- his suggestion of peacekeepers being located on the Drina River, made in the context of cease-fire discussions.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct; not of demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked a number of questions regarding the hostage situation -- well, I will use my -- I use that word advisedly. I know that there are differing views about it. The situation that you spoke about where your freedom of movement was impeded. And I don't know if it was quoting from a document or whether it was just put to you, but the notion that the refugees were revolted by Morillon, General Morillon, not having smelt the odour of death at Konjevic Polje may have led to their fears that you - I mean your party - might downplay the situation in Srebrenica. In the time that you were there and you were receiving information from Mihailov, did you ever hear of that particular concern? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at all. And I believe it incredible that the refugees in Srebrenica at that time would have had access to radios and would have even heard it. It was only the Tuzla authorities and the Bosniak Tuzla authorities and Bosniaks in Sarajevo who were very angry with General Morillon about that. Within the enclave, that was never -- never mentioned or never held against the General or raised in conversation or discussion with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record it was Cerska, the odour of death statement, not Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies. Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more, thank you, Mr. Jones, for your observation. You were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked if War Presidency or war committee members may have been present at the -- on the occasion on the 21st of March where the prisoner was released, and your evidence was you can't say if they were or were not. Were there any in the vehicle that you were in, as you travelled, from the point where the Mercedes turned up to the point where you collected --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Definitely not. There were only UN personnel in the -- I was in the armoured personnel carrier and General Morillon was in a Jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked about various entries relating to the prisoner during the course of your cross-examination, two entries in particular. I don't need to take you to them. I just remind you that you were cross-examined about the note the previous day and to the effect that General Morillon is going to seek the release of Serb prisoners, and then the following day, the 21st, that is in fact what happened.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. If Your Honours will just bear with me. Yes, yes. And you have also testified in examination-in-chief that there was a stretcher in the AP -- in the vehicle, whatever it was. Was that stretcher there by arrangement?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a permanent piece of the equipment in that vehicle. It was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Had General Morillon made arrangements to collect a prisoner and transfer him to the Serbs, would there have been any reason that you are aware of, that you know of or can think of, as to why you would not be informed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't particularly understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, if General Morillon had made arrangements at some prior stage, prior to the 21st, when the episode you spoke about occurred, to collect and transfer a prisoner from within the enclave to Serb-held territory, are you aware of any reason as to why you might not be informed of such arrangements?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need to show you the document, but this morning you were shown an Exhibit D -- which is now D224, 224. And in effect, it's the -- you've seen the document this morning and it deals with events at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And there is reference throughout the document to "Nasar," N-A-S-A-R, often in inverted commas. And you were also asked questions regarding your understanding of the name of the person that you were speaking to at Konjevic Polje. Can you enlighten as to why it is that you would have referred to this person Nasar, in inverted commas, in that report? Is there any reason that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't -- we weren't sure, as I said earlier, as to which was his first name, which was his surname. Because when we were in Konjevic Polje, the locals all referred to Naser, as opposed to Oric. And because I think somebody made the comment that, well, surely, Naser doesn't end in "ic," so again that is why we were puzzled. And we had only had the intelligence briefings that I had referred to previously. We had had the Serbs on a couple of occasions mention Colonel Oric and we had the mention by the Presidency. So we were in no particular doubt as to, broadly speaking, who this person was, but I wasn't sure whether I was correctly referring to him by Naser or Oric, and ranks were very -- on the Bosniak side, ranks were very loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Okay. I want to ask you about some questions that were put to you on the 15th. That's two days ago. You were being asked about, again, the situation, hostage situation or impeded movement situation, call it what you will. You were referred to an entry - again, I don't need to show it - in your diary. It's at 3442. That's the ERN number, and the quote that you were referred to was the quote that said, "Maybe Naser Oric could help."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And this is the way the -- it went: "The sentence paragraph 5 'Maybe Naser Oric could help,' isn't that expression of your opinion or whoever provided this information, that maybe -- that he could maybe help with the problems you had with the -- you had with the women's committee? "Yes, that is correct. "So you certainly didn't consider that he was behind what the women's committee was doing at that stage?" And you answered: "Not at that stage." You weren't asked if at any later stage you formed any other view, and that's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formed the opinion later that it was possible that -- sorry. We knew that the women's committee and the refugees had been marshaled by soldiers and there'd been whistles used to make the refugees surge forward at -- at times, and this had been controlled by soldiers. What we were not sure of at that time while we were at Srebrenica of who was who had given the orders and the instructions to the soldiers to behave like that. Was it the war committee? We were certain at the -- that Hajrudin was involved because he had -- his demeanour towards us. I think I recorded in the meetings that morning -- had changed completely and he wouldn't look us in the eyes any more. And so we believed that he was implicated in some way. We wondered whether, because these were soldiers who were involved, whether Naser Oric might have been involved, but we had no evidence one way or the other. The only thing I would add is that after the war there was a documentary, as there were many on Srebrenica, and I saw a documentary in which Hajrudin Avdic was interviewed and in which he said that he received instructions from Sarajevo to prevent General Morillon from leaving and to keep him in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours just give me a moment, I may be able to avoid a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were being asked questions regarding demilitarisation and the attitude of Colonel Oric and it ended up with this question from Mr. Jones and this answer from you. Question: "But despite his opposition he was in fact overruled, wasn't he? In the sense that there was a demilitarisation." And you answered: "That happened after I left." Now I think I know what you mean, but I want to be absolutely clear. Are you saying that he was -- yes, he was in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you saying that yes, in fact, he was overruled on the issue of demilitarisation? Or are you saying that happened after you left and you can't comment on it, you have no information about the process of demilitarisation and his attitude towards it.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell the court that in the conversation that he had with General Morillon an on the 17th, he was adamantly opposed to anything to do with demilitarisation. That I can confirm. That demilitarisation of Srebrenica took place after I left, as a matter of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the process which led to that demilitarisation, I'm obviously not in a position to be able to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I was driving at. Thanks very much. Could I ask you to remain outside the courtroom after you've finally left. I would like to speak to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I -- I am -- I'm certainly not proposing to re-cross-examine. There is, however, one question which arises from -- it's a linguistic issue and I fear if I don't clarify it there might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, please go ahead. Very soon the witness will be gone and then it will be too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, and it goes to what is called the sum or fallacy, and that's why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You were asked, page 96, line 24, about whether people were required to fight as opposed to being volunteers. And you were asked, "Did that situation apply as far as you could see in Srebrenica or not?" And you replied, "I was told that that situation pertained in Srebrenica." I just want to be clear you're not saying that applied to every single person, that they were required to fight.
