utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The vast majority of people were volunteers. But I had some reports of some people being -- some, as in a very small number, being "forced to fight."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has explained it already before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I thought for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: You have explained that you also, in the first half of February 1993, had rather intense discussion with the leadership of all three parties so to speak. And that you, during that period, heard the first accusations regarding the attacks and killing of people, civilian population, especially in Kravica, but I understand that was a more general accusation against what has happened out this enclave around Srebrenica. Do you know if General Halilovic became aware of those accusations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because when we were -- when accusations were made to us by one party about events that they -- actions they claimed the other side had done, we would, at the next meeting we had with the other side, would report that and say, the other side has made this claim. Would you -- can you explain, is there anything you can provide to help us understand that. If there is any truth in it, then please stop that action or give orders for that action to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of a response you got from the general?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two responses. The first one was, our forces are not attacking civilians. It is our civilians who are being attacked. And secondly, we are surrounded, our forces are surrounded. They have to make attacks in order -- in order to seize the means with which to -- with which to survive and defend ourselves. So that was one aspect. The second aspect is that, yes, we are carrying out military attacks against the Serb line of communication between Zvornik and Pale and Srebrenica, and those attacks are not only being made from out of the enclaves, but also being made from positions north of Sarajevo on the other side of that corridor that I showed you on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, did you, during that period, ever hear anything regarding burning down of villages, Serb villages, to make it impossible for them to be populated again by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We told Halilovic that -- and Ganic as well and Izetbegovic too, that those accusations were made, because initially the Serbs were general and Kravica itself was only mentioned about the middle of February. I would need to check my diary. Then when we had the specific name, we then reported that: "This is a specific accusation. Do you know about that?" And they said, "We have no knowledge of this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well then quite another question. You just mentioned that on the Bosnian side the ranks were very loose. Do you remember when you met the man you suppose was Colonel Oric, did he have any distinctions which shows him as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. No. No one in the Srebrenica pocket had any badges of rank that were -- that were identifiable or meaningful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, when you got this prisoner delivered so to speak, of course you have explained to us that he had all signs of starvation. Did he -- was he a wounded man? Could you see any sign of physical mistreatment, apart from, of course, the starvation and the situation that he was unable to walk?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had some bandages and his face was -- it was difficult to tell, because his face was so dark and he was -- he had obviously not shaved, but I think he had bandages as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: In the -- on the face, on the head or, do you recall anything about this? Or where it was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember where on his body the bandages were. What I do remember is that for some reason we -- or one of our soldiers pulled up his shirt, or whatever, to look at his stomach, because there was -- there was some -- I can't remember the reason why, but we looked at his stomach area, but I can't recall the reason why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I will be grateful to get some clarity, more clarity with regard to the different types of commanders or the language of commanders. In your diary, I could give you the page if you need, you speak of local commander and, did I understand you correctly that this context, local commander, was in terms of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Local to Srebrenica. In other words, under the influence of, maybe even under the orders of the War Presidency, but not in the more broad sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: If I may turn your attention to Exhibit D226, which was a special report on the situation in the Srebrenica area, and just keep you -- it was a report by Belgian general, you know whom I mean? Would you say the military commander tries to do something, but he is helpless, now to what person may he refer to in this context? The military commander, the question was -- general situation in Srebrenica. The local people seems to be quite healthy but the refugees are starving as they do not know the dropping zones distribution of the food is the first person to get it keeps it for himself.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the report by Major Denyft?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have been referring to the local military commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, in the -- if I may turn your attention to the extract from the book by Larry Hollingsworth. It was already cited this morning by the Defence. On page 2 -- 187, he would write: "Our guide ... was in uniform, was introduced as a military commander of the town." Now, you told us that there have been quite a few soldiers who guided you, but Hollingsworth goes on: "That he may have been, but we knew that the real defender of the region was Naser Oric whom we had met in Konjevici." Would you confirm this evaluation.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the relationship of the War Presidency and the man called, supposed to be Naser Oric. You already told us something, but what I wanted to make clear, when you had talks with him, with Naser Oric, did, at any time, he have some sort of deliberations back and forth with the members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of. My understanding is that he came in from outside the PTT building, that was before I was there, and that he then walked out. And it was only with -- with Colonel Oric that we spoke. There was nobody from the War Presidency present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And aside from the local commander, in terms of War Presidency and Colonel Oric, have there been any -- or did you observe any other military leaders who had a saying in your negotiations, or have there been any other people, calling themselves some sort of leader, had been connected or involved in your negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- I think his name is Bektic, Nedzad. I would need to refer to my diary to confirm the name, who was described as a local commander. And he certainly spent a lot of time subsequently with Major Dudley, and he and Major Dudley became quite friendly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was, did you observe that there had been deliberations between Colonel Oric and this person who you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw Colonel Oric have any conversations or discussions with any of the other people who we met in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So may I sum up this point: You would say that when Naser Oric made decisions, you did not observe that he had any -- needed any agreement with other people?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I asked for his experience, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the "needed" the "needed any the agreement." That is not something one can observe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now then another point is a question of crowd control. In your diary, on page -- what is it, ending in the 3464, you wrote: "There are 3 groupings in the area. Local population, refugees and soldiers. There is little coordination between the 3 groups." Now, was this merely a description or did you also want to express that this was a failure or a weakness which could have been avoided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was our opinion that there should have been more coordination and concern shown between the groups. And it was our opinion - very easy for us to say, very difficult in the circumstances, I appreciate - but it was our opinion that that was a major failing and would have made the situation much better in Srebrenica had there been much more coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Once more, I would like to turn your attention to the excerpts from the book by Larry Hollingsworth, where on page 212, he is also dealing with a situation that was difficult to control, the crowd getting on the trucks and so on, and he writes: "They had nothing else to do." The authorities. "Could the local authorities prevent the people from boarding the trucks?" And then he continues: "I felt that Naser Oric and his troops could, but that the rest could not." Could you confirm this assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's more complex than that. It's at two levels. One is, if the war committee had been more organised previously, as I had described earlier today, and built up a situation of trust with the refugees, such that the refugees believed and felt and trusted the war committee, that was one thing. The second thing is that Naser Oric wasn't there. And he may or may not have been able to control it, I don't know. But he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Judge Eser. I would love to put a lot of questions to you, Colonel, but that would mean keeping you another day here, which I am bent on avoiding at all costs. I wish to thank you for having accepted to come over and give testimony in this case against Naser Oric. It has taken a few days. It must have been extremely tiring. I must say you come out of it in the best manner possible. On behalf of the Tribunal on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser and on my own behalf, I wish to thank you once more. And on behalf of everyone presents here, I wish you a safe journey back home. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher and given all the assistance you require to facilitate your return home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've got one minute. Tomorrow I think we are sitting in the afternoon. Not in the morning. Correct me if I am wrong. Yes, Mr. Wubben, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have a new witness tomorrow. I don't suppose you're going to finish with that witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We need more time than only tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we will reconvene tomorrow afternoon at quarter past two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I make one comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I do so with the greatest reluctance, but I would like to just state the following. Our client obviously looks to the Bench to give him a fair trial, to consider the evidence presented by the parties, and of course to ask questions which help to clarify the evidence. If questions are to be put by part of the Bench which -- every one of which appears to be an attempt to create another building block for the Prosecution case, that's not fair to our client who has a right to look to Your Honours to be weighing the evidence as presented by the parties. I don't want to say any more on the matter there, but I would just implore Your Honours to ask questions which yes, clarify the evidence but which don't seek to help the Prosecution make their case against our client. I will say nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we discussed this earlier. I don't think you have a clear and correct vision of what the role of the judges in this Tribunal are according to the Statute, the documents, the official documents that created this Tribunal and also the practice of this Tribunal. Please, I repeat, do not for a moment consider that the role of the judges in this Tribunal is only a passive one, to listen and just to clarify things. We also have a responsibility to promote reconciliation and to ensure that the truth comes out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
